$comment: A `long double` READ keeps what the object held when it was read, and a `volatile long double` can be read and written (D-LIR-LONG-DOUBLE-LOAD-READ-THE-OBJECT-AFTER-IT-WAS-OVERWRITTEN, D-LIR-VOLATILE-LONG-DOUBLE-ACCESS-MOVED-ITS-ADDRESS-INTO-A-FLOAT-REGISTER). The discriminating arms are x86_64 and aarch64 Linux, where `long double` lives in a 16-byte memory home; each check reads an object, overwrites it, then uses the value it read, with distinct values so a read of the wrong object fails its own exit code (11–18, listed in `main.c`). ✔MEASURED 2026-09-19: gcc 13.3.0 and clang 18.1.3 run it to 42 at -O0 and -O2 on x86_64 and aarch64 Linux; the P68 round-7 base refused it on both Linux targets (the `volatile` accesses), and returned the OVERWRITTEN value for the same shapes without `volatile` in its release pipeline — `main.c` has the per-check detail. ⓘ Portable C: where `long double` IS `double` (Windows, Apple arm64) every check holds just the same. ★ The `release` arm: every starting value comes from a `volatile`, so the optimized pipeline cannot fold the reads away.
